lessons.title: On the farm
lessons.scenario: Smarty visits a sunny farm with Mia and Sam to meet the animals.

items.example: The pink pig is next to the cow.

questions.prompt: What can the yellow duck do?

practice.prompt: Listen, then choose what you heard.

A giraffe has a long nose.

practice.explanation: Giraffes have tall necks, elephants have long noses, monkeys love bananas, and tigers are orange and black.

lessons.title: Small and sea animals
lessons.scenario: Smarty and Zara explore the greenhouse plants and a big water basin.

items.example: A small mouse ate the cheese.
items.note: Say ‘mouse’ for one tiny animal with a long tail, and ‘mice’ for two or more.

items.example: The white rabbit has two long ears.

items.example: The green frog can jump and swim.

lines.speaker: Zara
lines.text: Is that a long snake under the chair?

practice.prompt: Say the sentence aloud.

story.hook: What did Ben see when he walked in the green forest?

image.describe: Smarty the black cat and Ben looking at travel photos on a table in the greenhouse showing a snowy mountain, a green forest with a bear, a cold river, a waterfall, a lake, and the sea.

lines.speaker: Smarty

lines.text: We went to a tall mountain with white snow!

lines.text: Yes! We walked in the green forest and saw a bear.

lines.speaker: Smarty
lines.text: Did you see water too?

questions.prompt: What was on the tall mountain?

questions.prompt: What did Ben see in the forest?

mission.setup: Smarty wants to hear about outdoor places you like.

turns.smarty: I love the green forest! Do you like the forest or the sea?
turns.hint: Say ‘I like the…’ and choose a place from this lesson.

turns.hint: Name the very high land with snow on top.

turns.smarty: Where do whales swim: in a lake or in the sea?

lessons.title: Describing animals
lessons.scenario: Smarty compares how fast, slow, strong, and dangerous animals are.

items.example: A horse can run fast.
items.note: Say ‘fast’ when someone or something moves with great speed.

items.example: A pig is slow, not fast.
items.note: Use ‘slow’ when something takes a long time to move.

items.example: A hungry lion is dangerous.
items.note: Say ‘dangerous’ when an animal or place can hurt you.

items.example: An elephant is big and strong.
items.note: Use ‘strong’ when someone or something has a lot of power.

items.example: A tiger is as fast as a lion.
items.note: Use ‘as … as’ to say two things are equal.

items.example: The rabbit is fast enough!
items.note: Put ‘enough’ after an adjective when it has the right amount.

grammar.title: as … as and … enough
grammar.explanation: Use ‘as + adjective + as’ when two animals are the same (as fast as, as strong as). Put ‘enough’ after an adjective when it has the right amount (fast enough, strong enough).
examples: A tiger is as fast as a lion.

practice.prompt: Which word means something can hurt you?
practice.explanation: ‘Dangerous’ means not safe—it can hurt you.

practice.prompt: Listen, then choose what you heard.
practice.audio: An elephant is big and strong.
practice.answer: An elephant is big and strong.
options: An elephant is big and strong.
An elephant is big and slow.
A lion is big and strong.
practice.explanation: Elephants are very strong.

practice.prompt: Match each word to its meaning.
practice.explanation: Fast and slow are opposites; dangerous means risky; strong means powerful.

practice.prompt: Which sentence means the tiger and the lion have the same speed?
practice.answer: A tiger is as fast as a lion.
options: A tiger is as fast as a lion.
A tiger is fast a lion.
A tiger is slow as a lion.
practice.explanation: Use ‘as + adjective + as’ to show two things are equal.

practice.prompt: Build the sentence comparing a tiger and a lion.
practice.answer: A tiger is as fast as a lion.
practice.explanation: Put ‘as’ both before and after ‘fast’.

practice.prompt: Complete the sentence.
practice.text: The small mouse is not ___ enough.
practice.explanation: ‘Enough’ comes right after the adjective ‘strong’.

practice.prompt: Complete the sentence.
practice.text: A snake can be ___.
practice.explanation: Some snakes can hurt you, so they are dangerous.

practice.prompt: Complete the sentence.
practice.text: The rabbit is ___!
practice.explanation: ‘Enough’ always goes after the adjective: ‘fast enough’.

practice.prompt: Say the sentence aloud.
practice.text: An elephant is strong, and a lion is dangerous.
practice.answer: An elephant is strong, and a lion is dangerous.
practice.explanation: Great job using ‘strong’ and ‘dangerous’!

story.hook: Is the green frog as fast as the white rabbit?

image.describe: In the greenhouse, Smarty the black cat and Ana watch a white rabbit hopping quickly past a green frog near potted plants.

lines.speaker: Ana
lines.text: Smarty, there is a white rabbit! It is fast!

lines.speaker: Smarty
lines.text: Yes, a rabbit is fast, and a green frog is slow.

lines.speaker: Ana
lines.text: Is the frog as fast as the rabbit?

lines.speaker: Smarty
lines.text: No, it is not fast enough! But the frog can swim.

lines.speaker: Ana
lines.text: What about a lion and a tiger?

lines.speaker: Smarty
lines.text: They are strong and dangerous!

questions.prompt: Is the green frog as fast as the white rabbit?
questions.explanation: Smarty says the frog is not fast enough.

questions.prompt: How is the green frog?
questions.explanation: Smarty says a green frog is slow.

questions.prompt: How are a lion and a tiger?
questions.explanation: Smarty says they are strong and dangerous.

mission.setup: Smarty is comparing animals with you. Answer using fast, slow, strong, dangerous, as fast as, or fast enough.

turns.smarty: An elephant is big. Is it strong?
accept: ^yes(?: an elephant is strong| it is(?: strong)?)?$
turns.hint: Say ‘Yes, it is strong’.

turns.smarty: Is a lion dangerous?
accept: ^yes(?: a lion is dangerous| it is(?: dangerous)?)?$
turns.hint: Say ‘Yes, a lion is dangerous’.

turns.smarty: Compare a tiger and a lion! Say: A tiger is as fast as a lion.
accept: ^a tiger is as fast as a lion$
turns.example: A tiger is as fast as a lion.
turns.hint: Say ‘A tiger is as fast as a lion’.

lessons.title: How it moves
lessons.scenario: Smarty watches how animals and friends move around the greenhouse.

items.example: The small mouse ran quickly.
items.note: Use ‘quickly’ to say someone does something fast.

items.example: The ducks swim happily in the lake.
items.note: Say ‘happily’ when someone does something with joy.

items.example: Sam walked carefully near the cold river.
items.note: Use ‘carefully’ when you do something with care so nothing goes wrong.

items.example: My brother played the drum loudly.
items.note: Say ‘loudly’ when someone makes a lot of noise.

items.example: Smarty walked quietly next to the mouse.
items.note: Use ‘quietly’ when someone moves or speaks with almost no sound.

items.example: That pig is too slow!
items.note: Put ‘too’ before an adjective when it is more than you want or need.

grammar.title: Adverbs of manner (-ly) and too
grammar.explanation: Add -ly to an adjective to tell how someone does an action (quickly, happily, carefully, loudly, quietly). Put ‘too’ before an adjective when it is more than good (too slow, too dangerous).

practice.prompt: Which word means with almost no sound?
practice.explanation: ‘Quietly’ means without making noise.

practice.prompt: Listen, then choose what you heard.
practice.audio: Smarty walked quietly next to the mouse.
practice.answer: Smarty walked quietly next to the mouse.
options: Smarty walked quietly next to the mouse.
Smarty walked loudly next to the mouse.
Smarty walked happily next to the mouse.
practice.explanation: Cats walk quietly when they see a mouse.

practice.prompt: Match each word to its meaning.
practice.explanation: Adverbs ending in -ly describe how an action happens.

practice.prompt: A mouse is fast. How did the mouse run?
practice.explanation: Use the adverb ‘quickly’ after the verb ‘ran’.

practice.prompt: Build the sentence about the ducks.
practice.answer: The ducks swim happily in the lake.
practice.explanation: ‘Happily’ tells how the ducks swim.

practice.prompt: Complete the sentence.
practice.text: Sam walked ___ near the cold river.
practice.explanation: Sam took care near the water, so he walked carefully.

practice.prompt: Complete the sentence.
practice.text: We cannot go by bus because it is ___.
practice.explanation: ‘Too slow’ means slower than we want.

practice.prompt: Complete the sentence.
practice.text: My sister played the trumpet ___.
practice.explanation: A trumpet makes a big sound, so she played it loudly.

practice.prompt: Say the sentence aloud.
practice.text: Smarty walked quietly, and the mouse ran quickly.
practice.answer: Smarty walked quietly, and the mouse ran quickly.
practice.explanation: Great contrast between quietly and quickly!

story.hook: Why did the white rabbit run quickly in the greenhouse?

image.describe: Inside the greenhouse, Mia walks quietly holding a glass of water near a sleeping white rabbit while Smarty the black cat watches and Omar sings loudly by the doorway.

lines.speaker: Mia
lines.text: Smarty, I walked quietly because the white rabbit was sleeping.

lines.speaker: Smarty
lines.text: Good! You walked carefully with that glass of water.

lines.speaker: Omar
lines.text: Hello, Mia! Hello, Smarty!

lines.speaker: Mia
lines.text: Shh, Omar! Do not sing loudly!

lines.speaker: Omar
lines.text: Sorry! The rabbit ran quickly!

lines.speaker: Smarty
lines.text: Haha! I am too slow for that rabbit!

questions.prompt: How did Mia walk with the glass of water?
questions.explanation: Mia walked quietly and carefully so she would not wake the rabbit.

questions.prompt: What did Mia tell Omar not to do loudly?
questions.explanation: Mia says: Do not sing loudly!

questions.prompt: Why could Smarty not catch the rabbit?
questions.explanation: Smarty says he is too slow for that rabbit.

mission.setup: Smarty is asking how things move. Use quickly, quietly, or too slow.

turns.smarty: When a baby is sleeping, how do you walk: loudly or quietly?
turns.hint: Say ‘Quietly’.

turns.smarty: When you see a fast rabbit, how does it run: slowly or quickly?
turns.hint: Say ‘Quickly’.

turns.smarty: Is a big pig fast, or is it too slow?
turns.hint: Say ‘It is too slow’.

lessons.title: Review
lessons.scenario: Smarty reviews natural places, describing animals, and how they move.

practice.prompt: Match each word to its clue.
practice.explanation: Mountains have snow, quickly means fast, tigers are dangerous, and lakes are surrounded by land.

A bear is strong a lion.
A bear is as strong a lion.

story.hook: What did Lily and Smarty see near the forest waterfall?

lines.speaker: Lily
lines.text: Smarty, we are in the forest near the waterfall!

lines.speaker: Smarty
lines.text: I walked carefully because the river is cold and fast!

lines.speaker: Lily
lines.text: There is a big brown bear near the water!

lines.speaker: Smarty
lines.text: A bear is strong and dangerous! Do not sing loudly!

lines.speaker: Lily

lines.speaker: Smarty

lessons.title: Our planet
lessons.scenario: Smarty, Mia, and Sam care for plants in the greenhouse and clean up the park.

items.example: I have a small brown seed in my hand.
items.note: Say ‘seed’ for the tiny part of a plant that grows into a new flower or tree.

image.describe: a paw holding small brown plant seeds above dark soil in a flowerpot

items.example: There is a big green leaf on the table.
items.note: Use ‘leaf’ for one green part on a tree or plant, and ‘leaves’ for many.

image.describe: a single bright green leaf with fine veins resting on a wooden table

items.example: This red rose is beautiful and sweet.
items.note: Say ‘rose’ for the pretty flower that is often red or pink.

image.describe: a blooming red rose with green leaves in a clay flowerpot

items.example: There is dirty rubbish in the park.
items.note: Use ‘rubbish’ for things people throw away that make a place dirty.

image.describe: crushed cans, paper, and empty plastic bottles scattered beside a park bench

items.example: We always recycle glass and bottles.
items.note: Say ‘recycle’ when you save glass, paper, or plastic to use again.

image.describe: Smarty the black cat putting a glass bottle into a green recycling bin

items.example: The river is dirty because there is pollution.
items.note: Use ‘pollution’ for dirty air, water, or land that hurts animals and plants.

image.describe: dark smoke and dirty water beside a factory contrasted with a clean green hill

practice.prompt: Which word is a pretty red or pink flower?

lessons.title: Nature walk
lessons.scenario: Smarty takes you on a nature walk by the forest and river to describe what you see.

items.example: Look at that! A tall giraffe is next to the tree.

items.example: This brown bear lives in the forest.
items.note: Use ‘It lives in…’ to tell where an animal has its home.

items.note: Say ‘It eats…’ to talk about an animal’s food.

practice.prompt: You suddenly see a huge whale in the sea. What do you say?
